sweep_summary: The single works with stress in the title (Feng 2016, 'Hanyu yulü yufa wenda') is a book on Mandarin Chinese prosodic grammar that Glottolog mis-assigned to Yulu-Binga by a computerised string match on 'yulu' (the record says so explicitly); relevance other-language, priority none. To make this search of works with stress in the title useful I downloaded the three open HAL manuscripts by Boyeldieu not yet held by the project (2007 Compound Verbs, the catalog's deciding source; 2008 'Yulu' qualification chapter; 2009 'Le quatrième ton du yulu', JALL 30) via HAL's file URLs with a non-browser user readers (HAL now serves an Anubis bot challenge to browser UAs; the Internet Archive was offline). Boyeldieu 2007 MS p. 7 verbatim confirms the catalog quote ('Yulu does not seem to have any kind of stress or prosodic feature that clearly marks word boundaries'). Boyeldieu 2009 §2 (MS p. 2) and 2008 §1.2 add a refinement: lexical units contrast one 'intense' syllable (seven vowel qualities x length) with 'non-intense' syllables where all vowel contrasts neutralise to ə (canonical CVCə, CəCVCə, VCə; polysyllables end in a non-intense syllable), and the tone system has four level heights. This is a vowel-reduction prominence, not accent, so the catalog's 'tonal' coding stands; recommend adding Boyeldieu 2009 §2 as a supporting/refining source. Gabjanda 1976 thesis (held by the project from the earlier reading) contains no Yulu stress statement beyond the accent-vs-tone framework note.

new_statements.quote: Les unités significatives du yulu sont généralement caractérisées par le contraste syntagmatique d'une syllabe intense – où s'opposent sept timbres dédoublés par une corrélation de longueur – avec une (des) syllabe(s) non intense(s) – où toutes les oppositions vocaliques sont neutralisées en un seul archiphonème ə : [...] Les polysyllabes sont donc généralement caractérisés par une syllabe finale non intense. [...] Le yulu distingue quatre hauteurs tonales fixes (ou 'plaines')
new_statements.translation: The meaningful units of Yulu are generally characterised by the syntagmatic contrast of one 'intense' syllable – in which seven vowel qualities, doubled by a length correlation, are opposed – with one (or more) 'non-intense' syllable(s) – in which all vowel oppositions are neutralised in a single archiphoneme ə. [...] Polysyllables are thus generally characterised by a non-intense final syllable. [...] Yulu distinguishes four fixed (or 'level') tone heights.

new_statements.reading: First-hand phonological description by the language's principal describer. Yulu is a four-height tone language (3 high / 2 mid / 1 low / 0 extra-low, with the fourth partly a depressor split). Word-level prominence is expressed not as stress but as a vowel-quality asymmetry: each lexical unit has one 'intense' syllable carrying a full vowel (7 qualities x length), all other syllables reduced to schwa; canonical forms VCə, CVCə (majority), CəCVCə, CVCəCVCə, so the full-vowel syllable is the penult in the commonest shapes. Boyeldieu never calls this stress, and in 2007 (p. 7, verified verbatim in, p. 8) states that Yulu 'does not seem to have any kind of stress or prosodic feature that clearly marks word boundaries'. So the catalog's classification 'tonal' is confirmed; the 2009 passage refines it (intense vs non-intense syllable = vowel-reduction prominence, not accent). Gabjanda 1976 (St Andrews PhD, held by the project) adds only the Mulderian accent-vs-tone theory passage and 'As for Yulu, distinctive para-phonotactic features [tones] are the most important' (printed p. 188); no Yulu stress statement.

new_statements.second_reader_bearing_note: No correction. Refinement only: the 2009 passage is a segmental/phonotactic description (full-vowel 'intense' nucleus vs schwa 'non-intense' nucleus), never framed as accent; the intense syllable is the penult in the majority VCə/CVCə/CəCVCə shapes, but reduplicated expressives CVCəCVCə carry two intense syllables and non-verbal lexemes drop the final schwa before pause ('forme réduite'), so it is not a culminative word-stress statement. Catalog stays 'tonal' with Boyeldieu 2007 p.7 as the deciding (only explicit) stress statement; 2009 §2 and 2008 §1.2 go in as supporting notes.

new_statements.relation_note: Compatible with the catalog's tonal classification and with the existing Boyeldieu 2007/2009 statements (no stress, tone-only word prosody). It adds an explicit accent-vs-tone framing in which tone is said to be the important para-phonotactic feature for Yulu, and an independent 1975 instrumental tone analysis. Its tone inventory (3 distinctive tones: level/rising/falling, from 4 phonetic levels) differs from Boyeldieu 2009's four level tone heights (3/2/1/0), but that is a tonal-analysis difference, not a stress claim. It also treats Yulu words as monosyllabic, whereas Boyeldieu 2009 gives CVCə etc. with a schwa syllable; again not a stress claim.
new_statements.rule_in_words: Gabjanda never states a word-stress or accent rule for Yulu. In his Mulderian framework 'accent' (contrastive para-phonotactic feature) and 'tone' (distinctive) are the two prosodic types; for Yulu he says the distinctive type (tone) is 'the most important' and analyses only tone: four phonetic pitch levels (High, Semi-High/Mid, Low-Mid, Low; 'confirmed by mingograms', p. 189) reduced to three distinctive tones, Tone I high level, Tone II rising, Tone III falling, established by minimal pairs such as /kad/ 'a person' vs 'salt' vs 'a donkey' (pp. 190-192). In the phonotactics chapter he treats the syllable as coinciding with the distributional unit and Yulu as 'monosyllabic and isolating' after Tucker 1940 (printed p. 163), so no polysyllabic word domain for stress is ever set up. The only 'stress' tokens in the Yulu-descriptive part are the Tucker & Bryan heading list ('phonetic, tone and stress', p. 148 region) and 'connotative stress' as a realizational feature distinguished from accent in the theory footnote (p. 33).
new_statements.exceptions: none; no stress rule is given so no exceptions
new_statements.identity_note: Gabjanda 1976 is by a native speaker (recordings made at SOAS in 1975), variety not named beyond 'Yulu'; Boyeldieu's work is on Yulu of the northern Central African Republic. No dialect distinction bears on the stress question.

new_statements.relation_note: Catalog classification tonal (Boyeldieu 2007 + 2009) is confirmed by the author's own 1987 sketch: four tone registers / thirteen patterns, no stress or accent vocabulary anywhere in the book. Compatible detail it adds relative to the statements held by the project: the four registers were already posited in 1987 (2009's 'quatrième ton' = the iB register and its link to voiced consonants, §2.16-2.17), the full-vowel + lax harmonising final vowel word shape (2009's intense/non-intense syllables) is described at pp.150-152 without any accentual interpretation, and tone has a demarcative (boundary-raising) function in noun determination (pp.141, 165-166), which sits well with 2007's remark tha…
new_statements.rule_in_words: Boyeldieu 1987 describes Yulu (Ouanda-Djallé, RCA) as a tone language: four level registers H, M, B(low) and iB (extra-low, historically split from *B under phonologically voiced consonants, §2.16-2.17) which alone or in pairwise combinations define thirteen lexical tone patterns over the canonical forms CV, CVV, (C)VCv, (C)VVCv (the last two by far the most numerous); rising patterns are almost exclusive to verbs; nouns undergo a demarcative tonal raising of their last component in determination contexts. Word shape: one full-vowel syllable followed by a short, lax final vowel harmonising with it (pp.150-152), i.e. the 1987 formulation of the 2009 'syllabe intense / non intense' asymmetry, never called accent. The words accent, accentué, accentuel, stress, intonation, proéminence, intense occur nowhere in the 280 pages ('tonique' only in 'personnels toniques' = independent pronouns): the book makes no word-stress statement.
new_statements.secondary_stress: none described (no stress described at all)
new_statements.exceptions: none about stress. Phonotactic notes seen: short-vowel CV words are almost exclusively grammatical, lexical items being CVV (p.137: exceptions cé 'là', da 'là-bas'..); a few grammatical words and two cardinals have a tense final vowel contrasting in timbre with the initial syllable (p.151); older speaker M. Sende pronounced CVCv/CVVCv words disyllabically with a final [a] or copy vowel where the young informants had no audible final vowel (Introduction p.20).
new_statements.identity_note: Boyeldieu 1987 describes the Yulu of Ouanda-Djallé (Central African Republic; data collected at Birao, Nov. 1984, from two young speakers plus an older speaker M. Sende), which he argues (Introduction 0.5-0.9) is the same language as the Yulu of Raga (Sudan) described by Santandrea 1970 and Gabjanda 1976; the book's other half treats Fer ('Kara' of Birao, kara1482).

(Topics in African Studies 9.) Köln: Rüdiger Köppe. HAL author MS halshs-00348130 (open:https://shs.hal.science/halshs-00348130/file/Qualif2_Yulu.pdf).
tone_statements.quote: Au plan phonologique la langue oppose, en syllabe intense, sept timbres vocaliques avec corrélation de longueur. Timbre et longueur sont intégralement neutralisés (Œ) en syllabe non intense. Le système tonal distingue quatre hauteurs fonctionnelles (haut : á, áa, moyen : å, åa, bas : à, àa, et infra-bas : ÷, ÷a).
tone_statements.translation: Phonologically the language contrasts, in the intense syllable, seven vowel qualities with a length correlation. Quality and length are entirely neutralised (ə) in non-intense syllables. The tone system distinguishes four functional heights (high: á, áa; mid; low: à, àa; and infra-low).
tone_statements.summary: 4 level tones (H, M, L, extra-low) on short/long vowels; grammatical tone (definite -H morphotoneme, person-indexed verb tone schemes).

tone_statements.citation: Boyeldieu, Pascal. 2006. Présentation des langues sara-bongo-baguirmiennes. Paris: CNRS-LLACAN (document électronique accompagnant le Lexique comparatif historique des langues SBB), 24 pp.https://llacan.cnrs.fr/SBB/Boyeldieu_SBB.pdf
tone_statements.quote: Plus récemment, Boyeldieu (2000) a proposé une classification historique, fondée sur la comparaison tonale de ces langues. [...] Le système *OCC, commun à ces dernières et notamment caractérisé par le développement d’un troisième registre tonal, se subdivise à son tour en cinq rameaux représentés par le yulu (langue unique), le groupe fer-gula koto, les autres parlers gula, le groupe nduga-luto (?) et l’ensemble des parlers ‘sara’.
tone_statements.translation: More recently, Boyeldieu (2000) proposed a historical classification based on the tonal comparison of these languages. [...] The *OCC system, common to the latter [the 'western' languages] and characterised notably by the development of a third tone register, subdivides in turn into five branches represented by Yulu (a single language), the Fer-Gula Koto group, the other Gula lects, the Nduga-Luto group (?) and the whole set of 'Sara' lects.
tone_statements.locator: pp.3-4 of 24, section on internal classification (schéma généalogique *SBB / *OCC)
tone_statements.summary: Comparative: SBB systems of 2, 3 or 4 level registers (4 = H/M/L/extra-low, the Yulu type); Yulu its own *OCC branch on tonal grounds.

tone_statements.citation: Boyeldieu, Pascal. 1998. Comparaison et reconstruction dans le domaine tonal : les langues sara-bongo-baguirmiennes. Faits de Langues 11-12 (Les langues d'Afrique subsaharienne, dir. S. Platiel & R. Kaboré), 99-110. Paris: Ophrys. DOI 10.3406/flang.1998.1201; open athttps://www.persee.fr/doc/flang_1244-5460_1998_num_6_11_1201
tone_statements.quote: Le caractère remarquable des propriétés tonales des langues SB В tient à plusieurs facteurs : diversité des systèmes (à deux, trois ou quatre registres pertinents), diversité des schemes tonals mis en œuvre dans les systèmes du même type et enfin régularité des correspondances tonales qui peuvent être dégagées. Le développement récent d'un quatrième registre (infra-bas) demeurant marginal, on concentrera l'exposé sur la comparaison des systèmes à deux et trois registres, l'hypothèse fondamentale étant qu'un sous-ensemble de langues "occidentales" a développé vers l'aigu un système originel à deux registres distinctifs, encore préservé sous cette forme dans les langues de l'est.
tone_statements.translation: The remarkable character of the tonal properties of the SBB languages is due to several factors: diversity of the systems (with two, three or four distinctive registers), diversity of the tonal patterns used within systems of the same type, and finally the regularity of the tonal correspondences that can be established. Since the recent development of a fourth (infra-low) register remains marginal, the discussion concentrates on comparing the two- and three-register systems, the basic hypothesis being that a subset of 'western' languages expanded upward an original system of two distinctive registers, still preserved in that form in the languages of the east.
tone_statements.locator: p. 102, section 2 'Les langues SBB' (Faits de Langues 11-12, 1998)
tone_statements.summary: Sara-Bongo-Bagirmi group: level-register tone systems of 2, 3 or (marginally) 4 registers; proto-SBB reconstructed with 2 registers, a third register innovated by a western subset (yulu, sar, gula); Lutos not named.

audit.reasoning: Quote check passes: both cited passages are verbatim in the held HAL PDFs at the stated pages. The tonal classification (four-height lexical tone, heavy lexical load) rests on a 2009 dedicated tone article in JALL by the language's main describer and is independently echoed by WALS 13A ('complex tone system', from Boyeldieu 1987) and by Boyeldieu 2005 fn.2 downloaded now; nothing suggests it is wrong. The weaker leg is the stress denial, which is a hedged aside in a 2007 compound-verb paper ('does not seem to have any kind of stress or prosodic feature that clearly marks word boundaries'); the two fuller descriptions that would settle whether the 'syllabe intense' is treated as an accent (Boyeldieu 1987 Geuthner monograph, 280 pp

sources.quote: Au plan phonologique la langue oppose, en syllabe intense, sept timbres vocaliques avec corrélation de longueur. Timbre et longueur sont intégralement neutralisés (Œ) en syllabe non intense. Le système tonal distingue quatre hauteurs fonctionnelles (haut : á, áa, moyen : å, åa, bas : à, àa, et infra-bas : ÷, ÷a).
sources.note: §1.2 typological sketch: four functional tone heights (high, mid, low, infra-low) marked on short and long vowels; 'intense' syllable with 7 vowels x length vs non-intense syllables neutralised to schwa; definite marked by a morphotoneme -H on the noun phrase; verbs carry a tone scheme that encodes both lexical identity and the person of the subject index (two person-linked tone schemes define verb classes); nominal/verbal derivation by tone (e.g. 'être aveugle' vs 'aveugle').

tone.translation: Phonologically the language contrasts, in the intense syllable, seven vowel qualities with a length correlation. sources.quote: Le caractère remarquable des propriétés tonales des langues SB В tient à plusieurs facteurs : diversité des systèmes (à deux, trois ou quatre registres pertinents), diversité des schemes tonals mis en œuvre dans les systèmes du même type et enfin régularité des correspondances tonales qui peuvent être dégagées. Le développement récent d'un quatrième registre (infra-bas) demeurant marginal, on concentrera l'exposé sur la comparaison des systèmes à deux et trois registres, l'hypothèse fondamentale étant qu'un sous-ensemble de langues "occidentales" a développé vers l'aigu un système originel à deux registres distinctifs, encore préservé sous cette forme dans les langues de l'est.

tone.locator: p. 102, section 2 'Les langues SBB' (Faits de Langues 11-12, 1998)
tone.translation: The remarkable character of the tonal properties of the SBB languages is due to several factors: diversity of the systems (with two, three or four distinctive registers), diversity of the tonal patterns used within systems of the same type, and finally the regularity of the tonal correspondences that can be established. Since the recent development of a fourth (infra-low) register remains marginal, the discussion concentrates on comparing the two- and three-register systems, the basic hypothesis being that a subset of 'western' languages expanded upward an original system of two distinctive registers, still preserved in that form in the languages of the east.
tone.summary: Sara-Bongo-Bagirmi group: level-register tone systems of 2, 3 or (marginally) 4 registers; proto-SBB reconstructed with 2 registers, a third register innovated by a western subset (yulu, sar, gula); Lutos not named.
